name: Diego Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mondays to Thursdays I'm on the bus along Canal Road by 7:40 for nursing lectures: anatomy, communication skills, a lot of reading. Fridays are a lab and a tutorial, and then I do ten hours picking orders at a pharmacy warehouse on Saturday and Sunday. I live with my mum, who cleans wards at St Aidan's hospital, and my sister Maya, who's 14. I do homework on the kitchen table after Maya's asleep, and I'm usually wrecked by Wednesday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd say good, because maybe hospitals can't use AI as an excuse to cut nurses. Nursing is people, and nothing on that card changes that. At the warehouse I'd tell the lads the scanners are fine as they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm more scared about money than about AI. My loan is already growing, my pay is fourteen hours a week, and the placements are unpaid. If AI is hype, then my worry is the normal one: can I afford three more years?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. I'd keep both weekend shifts, hand in my assignments on time and ask the student union rep about the placement hardship fund. I'd also keep helping Mum with Maya's school forms, because she's on her feet all day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired but steady. A bit relieved that nothing wild happens, but not calm, because the rent contribution I give Mum and the loan don't go away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes first if the warehouse cut your hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My bus pass, which is stupid because then I can't get to placement. After that I'd share Kasim's textbooks instead of buying my own. Mum would slip me forty quid and pretend it was nothing, and I'd hate that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd carry on as normal. Is there anything you'd try with AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I don't use it and I don't want to start. A girl on my course used it for a drug-dose question and it invented a number, and the tutor made an example of her. I'd rather learn it slowly, properly, the way nurses always have.

say: Nursing is **people**, so a bit of hype won't change what a ward needs.
I'd tell the lads at the warehouse the scanners are fine as they are.
think: I'm more scared of **money** than of AI, because the loan keeps growing.
Unpaid placements on top of weekend shifts are what really worry me.
do: Keep both weekend **shifts** at the pharmacy warehouse and keep my grades up.
Ask the student union rep about the placement **hardship fund**.
feel: Tired but steady, and only a little **relieved** because the money pressure stays.
S0.quote: My loan is already growing, my pay is fourteen hours a week, and the placements are unpaid.
fieldNote: Diego's worry is the **loan** and unpaid placements, not AI. He treats the card as a non-event and goes straight to money.
Firm **refusal** to use AI tools, with a concrete reason: a classmate's invented drug dose.

steps.text: Keep both weekend order-picking shifts at the pharmacy warehouse
Ask the student union rep about the placement hardship fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the usual story: the firms make the money and ordinary workers adjust. Hospital admin and booking would go to software first, and I'd say they'd better not use that to cut the nurses too. At uni I'd ask lecturers what our course will do about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, nursing looks safer than most because bodies need looking after. But the booking, the notes and the rotas go to software, and then wards get told to do more with fewer staff. That's what scares me, not a robot taking my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the nursing union as a student member, which is cheap. I'd learn to write clean patient notes by hand and in the system, since that's the part that'd be checked. And I'd keep my warehouse shifts, though I know the warehouse is exactly where the software goes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Mum's cleaning job at St Aidan's is contracted out, and a firm like that would swap staff for machines the minute it could. So it feels close to home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your mum's job fit into this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cleaning company already cut her hours twice. If they bring in floor-scrubbing machines, she's the one who goes, and then I'm paying more at home on my weekend wage. We've talked about it over dinner and she just says she'll find another ward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stay away from AI. Does that hold in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gets harder, yes. If hospitals expect it, I'd have to learn the one the hospital uses. But I'd want to be taught it on the course, with a tutor checking, not teach myself from videos.

say: The **firms** make the money and ordinary workers carry the change.
Software may take hospital booking first, and it must not become an excuse to cut nurses.
think: Nursing is safer than most jobs, but **staffing** will be squeezed once software does the admin.
The thing that scares me is the cuts, not a robot.
do: Join the nursing **union** as a student member.
Practise clean patient notes, since that is the part that gets checked.
Keep the warehouse shifts, though the software will hit them first.
feel: Uneasy, because the change is already close: **Mum's** contracted cleaning job could go to machines.
S1.quote: Mum's cleaning job at St Aidan's is contracted out, and a firm like that would swap staff for machines the minute it could.
fieldNote: Diego blames **employers**, not the technology. His family's money rests on a contracted cleaning job he expects to be cut.
He would use **AI** only if the course teaches it with supervision.

steps.text: Join the nursing union as a student member
Ask the tutor to teach the hospital's record system in class
Keep the warehouse shifts while they last

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a disaster waiting to happen because nobody has planned for it. Governments haven't, the hospital hasn't, my uni hasn't. I'd want the unions in the room before anything gets switched on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be frightened. Two years means I'm not even qualified yet, and the placements are mostly in my second year. Mum's job goes first, then maybe the warehouse, and Maya's still at school. I can't picture where the money comes from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the course because a nursing degree is the one thing I've got, and I'd push the union and my local politician to make sure patient care stays with people. I'd tell Mum to put her name down for any hospital job, not just cleaning. And I'd ask the careers office what the rules say about staying in the course if funding changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd not sleep. It's the speed: I can't plan anything in two years, and I'm the one my family counts on after Mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes because it's only two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything's squashed. I couldn't finish the degree before the thinking work is done by AI, so I'd be qualifying into a hospital that's still in chaos. But I'd also know robots are three years behind, so bedside care would last a bit longer than a desk job would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tech companies and the government that let them race. Nobody voted for this. I'd want a levy on the firms making money from it, paid into hospitals and into people like Mum.

say: Nobody has **planned** for this, not the government, the hospital or my university.
The unions must be in the room before anything is switched on.
think: Two years is too short: I'm not even **qualified** yet, and Mum's job goes first.
I can't see where the family's money comes from.
do: Stay on the **course**, because a nursing degree is the one thing I have.
Push the union and my local politician to keep patient care with people.
Tell Mum to apply for any hospital job, not only cleaning.
feel: **Alarmed** and not sleeping, because I can't plan anything and the family leans on me.
S2.quote: I'd be qualifying into a hospital that's still in chaos.
fieldNote: Diego's **alarm** comes from the household: his mum's contracted job goes first. He sees bedside nursing lasting longer than desk work.
He blames tech firms and government and wants a **levy** on profits.

steps.text: Stay on the nursing course and finish the first-year placement
Write to my local politician about keeping patient care with people
Go to every student union meeting on hospital jobs
Ask the careers office how funding rules would change

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do something, but only if somebody actually does it. I'd tell friends to sign the union petitions now, not later. Online I'd probably moan about the government for being slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In private I'm still anxious, but I'd feel I had a chance. I'd be qualified by about 2029, so I'd get a couple of years as a registered nurse before the robots reach the ward. I could save up. It's not safe, but it's a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, aim for a nursing role that is hands-on like emergency or elderly care, and pay Mum's rent share. I'd put fifty pounds a month away. And I'd lean on the union to push for a rule that a human nurse must be on every ward, which I'd vote for too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a bit steadier than the two-year one. At least I could look at the years in front of me and count them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why elderly care and emergency in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because they're messy and physical. Somebody has to lift an old man in bed 6 and talk to his daughter. Robots would take years to do that safely, and families would want a person there anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if the warehouse goes before you qualify?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have to find shifts in a care home as a healthcare assistant, which pays about the same and counts as experience. I'd already have asked about it by then.

say: Five years is enough to act, but only if **somebody** does something about it.
I'd tell friends to sign the union petitions now.
think: I'd still be **anxious**, but a registered nurse for a couple of years before robots reach the ward is a plan.
Saving fifty pounds a month would be a start.
do: Finish the degree and aim for **hands-on** work like emergency or elderly care.
Put fifty pounds a month away and keep paying Mum's rent share.
Back a rule that a human nurse is on every ward.
feel: Anxious, but **steadier** than the two-year picture because the years can be counted.
S3.quote: Somebody has to lift an old man in bed 6 and talk to his daughter.
fieldNote: More time turns Diego's fear into a **plan**: qualify, choose hands-on work, save a little.
He picks elderly and **emergency** care because robots would be slowest to do them safely.

steps.text: Save fifty pounds a month from the weekend wage
Vote for and campaign on a human-nurse-per-ward rule
Apply for care home assistant shifts as a backup to the warehouse

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time, and I'd say that out loud: long enough to do the degree, get experience and maybe even buy a place. I'd still tell people the unions have to start talking about it now, because ten years goes fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm a little less afraid. I'd be a nurse in my late twenties with robots arriving around thirty-two or so. But I don't trust the government to use the time well, so I'd be anxious anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, work as a nurse for a few years and look at a specialism that needs a person, like palliative care. I'd save, help Maya through school and see what the union is doing. I wouldn't change anything big yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly okay in the day, nervous at night. Ten years feels like time, but I know I'd waste some of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently if you knew about the ten years in advance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get Maya to pick a subject that needs people too, and I'd get Mum on a training course now, while she's still got energy. I'd not spend money I don't have. Mostly I'd just say no to things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make ten years go badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If everyone just waits. Governments say they'll deal with it and then nothing happens until year nine. I'd want the nursing union to demand a plan every year, in public.

say: Ten years is **long** enough to qualify, get experience and maybe buy a place.
The unions still have to start talking about it now.
think: I'd be less afraid, but I don't **trust** the government to use the time well.
Robots would reach the ward when I'm about thirty-two.
do: Finish the degree and work as a nurse, then look at **palliative** care.
Get Mum onto a training course while she still has energy.
Help Maya choose a school subject that still needs people.
feel: Okay in the day and **nervous** at night, because I'd know I might waste some of the years.
S4.quote: I'd get Mum on a training course now, while she's still got energy.
fieldNote: Diego has time but not **trust**: his fear is that institutions wait until year nine.
His planning is for the **household**, with his mum's training and his sister's subjects as concrete moves.

steps.text: Look at a palliative care specialism after qualifying
Get Mum onto a training course now
Ask the nursing union to demand a public plan every year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Two years, easily. That's the one where I'd have no time to qualify or fix anything. What would help is people getting told early, a training place for Mum, and the hospitals and unions agreeing that nursing stays a human job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like my mum are never in the picture. Everyone talks about graduates and coders, and nobody asks the person pushing the cleaning trolley.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about graduates and coders, and nobody asks the person pushing the cleaning trolley.
portrait: Diego is a 19-year-old **nursing** student who lives with his mum and sister and works weekends at a pharmacy warehouse.
He is progressive and distrusts firms and government, and he avoids AI tools after seeing a classmate's invented drug dose.
His fear is for the household: his mum's contracted cleaning job would go first.
With more time he turns fear into a plan: qualify, pick hands-on care and save.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries him most because he would not even be qualified and his family would lose income first.
whatWouldHelp: Early warning, a **training** place for his mum, and a firm agreement that nursing stays a human job.
